title: Greedy Best-First in Alfama: Fast Route Magic
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race through Lisbon’s Alfama street layout, always expanding the node that looks closest to the goal. The visualization highlights how heuristic-driven search moves quickly—but can be tricked by steep turns and disconnected shortcuts.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Greedy Best-First in Lisbon (Alfama)!

In this visualization, the agent explores a street graph using a priority queue ordered by the heuristic h(n) = estimated distance from node n to the target. 🚦 Instead of considering full path cost like Dijkstra/A*, Greedy Best-First uses only “what seems nearest right now,” so f(n)=h(n). That’s why it often looks incredibly fast on real map-like networks—until local “pretty” corridors lead away from the globally shortest route. 📉

🔍 Graph theory view: each intersection is a node and each road segment is an edge; the algorithm performs a heuristic-guided best-first search on this weighted graph (or effectively weighted geography). On real street maps, landmark-like cliffs, narrow alleys, and one-way constraints can cause heuristic traps—great for understanding how heuristics shape exploration.

👉 Want the shortest-path version too (A* vs Greedy)? Comment “A*” and I’ll make a follow-up reel. 💬📹
fb_caption:
🚗💡 Greedy Best-First is a heuristic graph search that always expands the “most promising” intersection next—based on estimated distance to the goal. Here, we model Alfama’s streets as a graph (nodes = intersections, edges = road segments) and watch how the search frontier moves using h(n) only.

📌 Learn how heuristic-driven exploration differs from cost-aware methods, then share this reel with a friend who loves maps, coding, or algorithms!

Greedy Best-First pathfinding on a REAL street map: Lisbon (Alfama)! 🗺️🚦

In this video/Short, we visualize how Greedy Best-First uses ONLY the heuristic h(n) (estimated distance to the goal) to choose the next node from the priority queue. Watch the search frontier move through a graph of intersections and road segments—and see why Greedy can be fast, yet sometimes not globally optimal.
